title: Indirect statement: accusative and infinitive, and quod, quia, quoniam

objectives.can: Read an accusative and infinitive as a reported statement and give the time of the infinitive relative to the main verb; read the Bible's quod, quia and quoniam clauses the same way.

explanation.summary: Latin reports what someone says, thinks, knows or sees in two main ways. The classical way puts the reported subject in the accusative and the verb in the infinitive. The Latin Bible, following the Greek, very often uses a clause with *quia*, *quoniam* or *quod* and an ordinary verb instead. A reader must know both.

sections.heading: The accusative and the infinitive
body: After a verb of saying, thinking, knowing or perceiving, the thing reported is put in a special form. English says 'they say that he is alive'. Latin drops the word 'that', puts the subject of the report into the accusative and turns its verb into an infinitive. In Luke 24:23 the women report angels *qui dicunt eum vivere*. The word *eum* is the subject of *vivere*: 'who say that he is alive'. It is not the object of *dicunt*, though it stands right beside it.

The predicate of the infinitive, if there is one, is accusative too, because it agrees with the subject. In Matthew 16:13 Jesus asks *Quem dicunt homines esse Filium hominis?* The subject of *esse* is *Filium hominis*, and *quem* is its predicate. *homines* is nominative, the subject of *dicunt*. A literal rendering is 'Whom do men say the Son of man to be?'.

Word order does not tell you which accusative is the subject. In Acts 8:37 the Ethiopian answers *Credo Filium Dei esse Jesum Christum*. Both *Filium Dei* and *Jesum Christum* are accusative. The sense decides: he believes that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, so *Jesum Christum* is the subject and *Filium Dei* the predicate. When a subject and a predicate are both nouns, look for which one the sentence is about.

sections.heading: The tense of the infinitive: time relative to the main verb
body: The tense of an infinitive in indirect statement does not give absolute time. It gives time relative to the main verb. A present infinitive means the same time as the verb of saying. A perfect infinitive means earlier. A future infinitive means later.

In Luke 24:23 both are in one verse. The women came back *dicentes se etiam visionem angelorum vidisse*, saying that they had seen a vision: the perfect *vidisse* is earlier than the saying. And the angels *dicunt eum vivere*: the present *vivere* is simultaneous with *dicunt*. The same present infinitive would be 'was alive' if the main verb were past, because it still means 'at the same time as the saying'.

The future infinitive is made of a future participle and *esse*: for example *futura esse*, 'were going to be', in Acts 26:22, where Paul says he preaches only what the prophets spoke of as *futura esse*. Compare the perfect infinitive in 2 John 7: those who do not confess *Jesum Christum venisse in carnem*, that Jesus Christ has come, an event earlier than the confessing.

sections.heading: The reflexive: se for the speaker
body: When the subject of the reported statement is the same person as the subject of the verb of saying, Latin does not use *eum* or *eos*. It uses the reflexive *se*. In 1 John 2:9, *Qui dicit se in luce esse* means 'he who says that he himself is in the light'. In Revelation 2:2 the false apostles are *qui se dicunt apostolos esse*: those who say that they are apostles. *se* is the subject of *esse*, and *apostolos* is the predicate, accusative to agree with it.
If the writer had used *eum*, the 'he' of the report would be somebody else. This is why *se* matters for meaning.

sections.heading: Quia, quoniam, quod: the Bible's clauses
body: Instead of the accusative and the infinitive, the Vulgate very often uses a clause beginning with *quia*, *quoniam* or *quod*, with a finite verb. In John 3:2 Nicodemus says *scimus quia a Deo venisti magister*: 'we know that you have come from God as a teacher'. The verb *venisti* is an ordinary indicative with its own subject, and *quia* means 'that'. In 1 John 5:20 the construction is the same with *quoniam*: *scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit*.

These words usually mean 'because'. Here they mean 'that', and only the sense of the verb before them tells you: after a verb of saying, knowing or seeing, they open the report. This use follows the Greek word for 'that' in the New Testament. Classical authors usually preferred the accusative and infinitive for such reports, but both are good Latin in the Church's books, and the patristic authors use the infinitive and the clause alike.

The mood in a *quia* or *quoniam* clause varies. After a present main verb the indicative is common, as in *scimus quia ... venisti*. After a past main verb the subjunctive is often used, as in Matthew 2:16, where Herod sees *quoniam illusus esset a magis*, 'that he had been tricked by the wise men'. The subjunctive here marks the content as reported, as one person's perception. It does not mean that the fact is doubtful.

sections.heading: Reading a report
body: Three questions find a report. First, is there a verb of saying, knowing, thinking or perceiving? Second, is there either an accusative beside an infinitive or a *quia*, *quoniam* or *quod* with a finite verb? Third, which accusative is the subject, and what time does the infinitive show? Answer these before you translate, and the English will follow.

misunderstandings: Taking the accusative beside the main verb as its object. In *dicunt eum vivere* the word *eum* is the subject of *vivere*: they say that he is alive. They do not say 'him'.
Reading *quia* and *quoniam* as 'because' after verbs of saying and knowing. There they usually mean 'that'. The clue is the verb before them.
Using word order to decide which accusative is the subject. Latin word order is free. In *Credo Filium Dei esse Jesum Christum* the sense decides.
Treating the infinitive's tense as past, present or future in itself. It is relative to the main verb: a perfect infinitive is earlier than that verb, a present is simultaneous, a future is later.

deeper.heading: Two ways to report, and why
body: Early Latin has reports with *quod* and *quia* in a few places, but the accusative and infinitive was the standard classical form. Where the New Testament uses a clause with the Greek word for 'that', the Latin translators often copied its shape with *quia* or *quoniam*, and they sometimes used the infinitive where the Greek has a clause. The usage then spread into the Christian writers, who can be found with both forms close together.
Grammarians describe the details differently, and a student does not need to decide among them. What matters is that in a Christian text neither form can be ignored.

examples.analysis: Two reports in one verse. *dicentes se ... vidisse*: the women say that they themselves had seen a vision, and the perfect infinitive *vidisse* is earlier than the saying. *qui dicunt eum vivere*: *eum* is the accusative subject of the present infinitive *vivere*, which is simultaneous with *dicunt*.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: This man came to Jesus by night, and said to him: Rabbi, we know that thou art come a teacher from God; for no man can do these signs which thou dost, unless God be with him.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: Gives the cause: 'we know, because you have come'
Introduces the content of the knowledge: 'we know that you have come'
check.explain: After a verb of knowing, *quia* opens the report, like English 'that'. Latin used the finite verb *venisti*, not an infinitive, in this construction.

check.prompt: *Si dixerimus quoniam peccatum non habemus* (words 0–5): how is the content of the saying given?

quoted.title: 1 John
quoted.english: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: By a quoniam clause with a finite verb
check.explain: The report is a *quoniam* clause with *habemus* in the indicative. A classical writer would more likely have written an accusative and infinitive. Both mean the same.

check.prompt: *Herodes videns quoniam illusus esset a magis* (words 1–7): what does *quoniam* introduce, and what does the subjunctive *esset* tell us?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: Then Herod perceiving that he was deluded by the wise men, was exceeding angry; and sending killed all the men children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the borders thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: What Herod saw, with the subjunctive marking it as his perception, not as extra doubt
A reason, with the subjunctive showing it is doubtful
A purpose, with the subjunctive marking aim
A condition, with the subjunctive showing it is contrary to fact
check.explain: After *videns* the clause is the content of what he saw. The subjunctive after a past main verb often marks the content as reported from his point of view; it does not say that the fact was doubtful, since he had indeed been tricked.

reading.why: Four verses of reports with *quoniam*: 'we know that', 'we testify that', 'whoever confesses that'. The same shape recurs, so that you can see the construction several times in a short space.
